title: How A became 440
hook: For centuries, the note A could mean a different pitch in every city.
peek: Today orchestras around the world tune to an A of about 440 vibrations a second. For most of history there was no such agreement, and A drifted from town to town and decade to decade. A 1939 conference in London finally settled on 440.
lede: When an orchestra tunes up, the oboe plays an A, usually at 440 vibrations a second. That number is surprisingly young. For centuries there was no shared standard, and an A in one city's church organ could sit noticeably higher or lower than an A across the border. Only in 1939 did an international meeting in London agree that A should be 440.

bullets.text: Surviving organs and tuning forks show As ranging from below 400 to above 460 vibrations a second. That gap is close to a semitone or more, so music played in one place could sound noticeably flatter or sharper somewhere else.
The trumpeter John Shore is credited with inventing the tuning fork in 1711. A fork said to have belonged to Handel sounds an A of about 422, well below today's standard.
In 1859 the French government fixed A at 435, partly to rein in pitch that had crept upwards and strained singers' voices. Many countries followed, but others did not, and the variety continued.

An international standards meeting in London in 1939 recommended 440. It became an ISO standard in 1955. Many orchestras still tune slightly higher, often 442 or 443, for a brighter sound, so the standard is followed loosely.
